questions.question: Compare SAST vs DAST vs IAST vs SCA vs secrets scanning vs container/IaC scanning — where does each fit in a pragmatic secure-by-default pipeline, and how do you avoid alert fatigue?
questions.title: Security Scanning Compared: SAST, DAST, IAST, SCA, Secrets, Container, IaC — and Token Formats
questions.direct_answer: **Each tool finds a different class of bug; none is sufficient alone, and more tools ≠ more security if nobody triages them.** **SAST** (Semgrep, SonarQube, CodeQL) analyzes source for bug patterns — fast, early, noisy; best for injection, auth flaws, insecure API use. **SCA** (Snyk, Dependabot, Trivy, OSV-Scanner) checks dependencies for CVEs — **the highest-ROI scanner** since most real incidents are dependency CVEs. **DAST** (ZAP, Burp) tests the running app for OWASP Top 10 — catches misconfigs SAST can't see; slow, runs against staging. **IAST** (Contrast, Seeker) instruments the runtime — best accuracy, harder to deploy. **Secrets scanning** (Gitleaks, TruffleHog, GitHub Advanced Security) prevents AWS keys in commits. **Container scanning** (Trivy, Grype, Clair) checks OS + Java deps in images. **IaC scanning** (Checkov, tfsec, KICS) catches misconfig in Terraform/CloudFormation. For frameworks: **OWASP Top 10** is the broad checklist; **ASVS** is a tiered requirement standard for depth; **NIST 800-53 / SOC 2 / ISO 27001** are compliance mappings, not code checks. For **session vs JWT vs OAuth2 tokens**: session is simplest and easiest to revoke; JWT scales stateless but revocation is painful; OAuth2 + OIDC with opaque tokens at the boundary + short-lived JWTs internally is the modern compromise. The anti-pattern: stacking 8 scanners, none triaged, 2000 open findings, real vulnerabilities buried in noise.

interviewer_intent.soft_skills: Pragmatism, security depth, trade-off judgment, pipeline thinking
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating all scanners equivalent; over-indexing on SAST; no triage; ignoring SCA (biggest real risk); JWT dogma
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Map each scanner to bug class; SCA as highest ROI; triage strategy; ASVS vs OWASP; session vs JWT vs OAuth2 trade-offs

sections.title: Why Compare Security Tools and Standards Side-by-Side
sections.content:
Every engineering team gets the same pitch: "enable our scanner, it finds everything." Reality: scanners find different bug classes with different false-positive rates and different operational costs. Stacking 8 scanners without triage makes you **less** secure — real vulnerabilities get lost in the noise.

**The broad categories**
- **SAST (Static Application Security Testing)** — analyzes source code for patterns
- **DAST (Dynamic Application Security Testing)** — probes a running app
- **IAST (Interactive Application Security Testing)** — runtime instrumentation that combines both
- **SCA (Software Composition Analysis)** — checks open-source dependencies for known CVEs
- **Secrets scanning** — finds credentials committed to source
- **Container image scanning** — OS + app deps in Docker images
- **IaC scanning** — misconfigurations in Terraform / CloudFormation / Kubernetes YAML
- **Runtime security** — eBPF-based (Falco), anomaly detection, workload behavior
- **Pen testing** — humans with expertise

**Frameworks and standards (not scanners)**
- **OWASP Top 10** — the starting checklist for web app risks
- **OWASP ASVS** — verification standard with levels (L1 opportunistic, L2 standard, L3 advanced)
- **NIST CSF / 800-53** — government/compliance controls
- **SOC 2 / ISO 27001** — auditable frameworks; not code-level
- **CWE/CVE** — bug taxonomy / vulnerability identifiers
- **CIS Benchmarks** — hardening guides for OS, K8s, cloud

**Token / session formats**
- **Session (cookie + server store)** — simplest, easy to revoke, stateful
- **JWT (signed claims)** — stateless scale, revocation painful, token bloat
- **OAuth2 + OIDC** — delegation framework, opaque tokens at edge, JWTs internally

**What interviewers test**
- Do you know which scanner catches which bug class?
- Do you know SCA is the biggest real-world risk?
- Can you design a pipeline without alert fatigue?
- Do you understand OWASP Top 10 vs ASVS as different tools?
- Do you grasp session / JWT / OAuth2 trade-offs — not dogma?

sections.title: SAST, DAST, IAST — What Each Catches
sections.content:
**SAST (Static Application Security Testing)**
- Tools: Semgrep, SonarQube, CodeQL (GitHub Advanced Security), Checkmarx, Fortify, SpotBugs + FindSecBugs
- **Catches**: SQL injection patterns, unsafe deserialization, crypto misuse (DES, MD5), XSS sources/sinks, hardcoded secrets, insecure config calls
- **Misses**: logic flaws, misconfig, runtime state, dependency CVEs
- **Strengths**: fast, runs in PR CI, language-aware, can cite line numbers
- **Weaknesses**: high false positives, context blindness, noisy on legacy codebases
- **How to use well**: PR-scoped (only scan changed files); curated rule sets (Semgrep OWASP/CWE packs); severity-based gating
- **Triage discipline**: triage high-severity within 48h; medium within sprint; suppress confirmed false positives with rationale in code
- **Semgrep advantage**: lightweight, customizable rules, great FP rate; pairs with CodeQL for depth

**DAST (Dynamic Application Security Testing)**
- Tools: OWASP ZAP, Burp Suite, Netsparker, Acunetix, Nuclei
- **Catches**: runtime vulns — auth bypass, CSRF, session issues, open redirects, cookie misconfigs, SSL issues, some OWASP Top 10
- **Misses**: code paths not exercised by the scanner, bugs requiring specific business workflows
- **Strengths**: sees the actual running app, catches misconfig SAST can't
- **Weaknesses**: slow (hours), requires running env, needs good test coverage to exercise surfaces
- **How to use**: nightly or weekly against staging; parameterized for logged-in flows; seeded with API contracts (OpenAPI-aware scans)
- **Nuclei niche**: templated scans for CVEs in known tech stacks

**IAST (Interactive)**
- Tools: Contrast Security, Seeker, Hdiv
- **How it works**: instruments the running JVM, sees both code paths and runtime data
- **Catches**: combines SAST + DAST; very low FP since it correlates source and runtime
- **Strengths**: best accuracy, integrates into CI/staging test flows
- **Weaknesses**: commercial only (usually), runtime overhead, complex setup
- **When to use**: when SAST FP rate is too high and you have budget

**The practical stack for most Java teams**
- **PR CI**: Semgrep (fast) + CodeQL (deep, weekly) + SCA + secrets + IaC — must pass
- **Nightly**: SonarQube with quality gates; ZAP against staging
- **Runtime**: Falco for eBPF-based anomalies; Datadog ASM or Contrast for RASP/IAST
- **Quarterly**: human pentest on critical flows

sections.title: SCA, Secrets, Container, IaC Scanning
sections.content:
**SCA (Software Composition Analysis)** — usually the **highest-ROI** scanner
- Tools: Snyk, GitHub Dependabot, OSV-Scanner, Trivy (deps), Mend (WhiteSource), Sonatype IQ
- **What it does**: scans `pom.xml`, `build.gradle`, `package-lock.json`, `go.sum` for known CVEs
- **Why it matters**: Log4Shell, Spring4Shell, Struts — real incidents almost always dependency CVEs, not custom code SQL injection
- **Reachability analysis**: newer tools (Snyk, Endor Labs) check if vulnerable code is actually called — cuts FPs 50–80%
- **License compliance** (GPL in proprietary code) — often bundled
- **SBOM generation** (Syft, CycloneDX, SPDX format) — compliance and supply-chain transparency
- **Policy**: auto-merge low-risk patch updates (Renovate, Dependabot); human review for majors; block commits introducing HIGH/CRITICAL CVEs without a remediation

**Secrets scanning**
- Tools: Gitleaks, TruffleHog, GitHub Advanced Security, GitGuardian, detect-secrets
- **Catches**: AWS keys, tokens, passwords in commits, config files, environment variables
- **Where to run**:
  - Pre-commit hook (fastest feedback)
  - CI on every PR (safety net)
  - Historical scan on main (catch old leaks)
- **When a secret leaks**: rotate immediately (AWS IAM keys, DB password, API token) — scanners alone don't fix it; you need an **incident runbook**
- **Preventive**: use secret managers (AWS Secrets Manager, Vault), environment injection at runtime, never commit `.env` files

**Container image scanning**
- Tools: Trivy, Grype, Clair, Anchore, Snyk Container
- **Catches**: OS package CVEs (Alpine apk, Debian apt, RHEL rpm), Java deps in fat JARs
- **Run**: at build time; fail if HIGH/CRITICAL; policy: rebuild weekly to pick up new CVEs on old base images
- **Distroless / Wolfi** base images have fewer packages → fewer CVEs
- **Image signing** (Cosign, Sigstore) — prove provenance; admission controllers can enforce

**IaC scanning**
- Tools: Checkov, tfsec, KICS, Terrascan, Snyk IaC
- **Catches**: open S3 buckets, overly permissive IAM, unencrypted RDS, K8s pods running as root, missing network policies, ingress wide open
- **Run**: PR CI on Terraform / CloudFormation / Kubernetes YAML
- **Policy as code**: OPA / Gatekeeper enforces at runtime what IaC scan finds at pre-deploy
- **Baseline of value**: catches 80% of S3 / IAM misconfigs that lead to breaches

**Runtime security (beyond scanning)**
- **Falco / eBPF** — detect anomalous syscalls, file reads, network connections
- **RASP (Runtime Application Self-Protection)** — Contrast, Datadog ASM block attacks in-process
- **WAF (Cloudflare, AWS WAF)** — edge defense against OWASP Top 10 patterns

sections.title: Frameworks: OWASP Top 10 vs ASVS vs NIST vs SOC 2
sections.content:
These are **not scanners** — they're standards and taxonomies that shape your scanner rules and audit posture.

**OWASP Top 10**
- Broad risks list updated every 3–4 years (2021 current; 2025 expected)
- Categories: Broken Access Control, Crypto Failures, Injection, Insecure Design, Security Misconfig, Vulnerable Deps, Auth Failures, SSRF, Logging Failures, SSRF
- **Use**: baseline security training; minimum scanner coverage; prioritization
- **Limit**: list, not a standard — doesn't tell you "passed/failed"

**OWASP ASVS (Application Security Verification Standard)**
- Tiered requirement catalog — **the right standard for depth**
- Levels: L1 opportunistic (SaaS, low-value), L2 standard (business apps), L3 advanced (healthcare, finance, critical infra)
- 14 chapters covering auth, session, access control, validation, crypto, logging, etc.
- **Use**: define your target level; map scanner rules + tests to requirements; track coverage
- ASVS L2 is the realistic target for most business apps; L3 for regulated industries

**NIST CSF / 800-53 / 800-171**
- Government-focused controls; required for federal contractors (CMMC, FedRAMP)
- Broader than app security; covers org policy, asset management, IR
- **Use**: if you're selling to government or need FISMA/FedRAMP; otherwise too heavy for app-level

**SOC 2 / ISO 27001**
- Auditable trust frameworks for SaaS companies
- Focus: controls, policies, evidence — not code
- SOC 2 Type II — 6+ months of evidence on implemented controls
- Requires: change management, access review, incident response, monitoring, vendor management
- **Use**: B2B SaaS customer demand

**CIS Benchmarks**
- Hardening guides — OS (RHEL, Ubuntu), K8s, Docker, AWS, Azure, GCP
- **Use**: benchmark your images and clusters; many tools (Trivy, kube-bench) check CIS

**CWE / CVE**
- CWE = bug class taxonomy (`CWE-89: SQL Injection`)
- CVE = specific vulnerability in specific software (`CVE-2021-44228: Log4Shell`)
- Scanners output CWE/CVE identifiers; use for triage, patch tracking, reporting

**How to stitch them together**
- ASVS defines **what** — your security requirements catalog
- Scanners + tests verify **how** each requirement is met
- OWASP Top 10 keeps eyes on the most exploited risks
- SOC 2 / ISO audits the **process** (change mgmt, IR, access review)
- NIST only if you need it for compliance

sections.title: Session vs JWT vs OAuth2/OIDC Tokens
sections.content:
A perennial interview debate with no single right answer.

**Session (cookie + server-side store)**
- Client gets a random session ID cookie; server looks up session state (Redis, DB)
- **Strengths**: trivial to revoke (delete server entry), small cookie, no crypto drama
- **Weaknesses**: stateful — every request hits session store; harder cross-domain
- **Best for**: traditional web apps, server-rendered UIs, anywhere with one backend

**JWT (JSON Web Token)**
- Self-contained signed (or encrypted) token with claims; stateless verification
- **Strengths**: stateless scale, works across services without session store lookup, good for microservices
- **Weaknesses**:
  - **Revocation pain** — tokens live until expiry; blacklist or short-lifetime + refresh
  - **Bloat** — claims + signature = larger cookie/header than session ID
  - **Secret management** — symmetric HS256 secret shared widely is risky; prefer RS256/ES256 with key rotation
  - **`alg:none` bug** — legendary JWT library flaw; always enforce algorithm allowlist
- **Best for**: microservices internal auth with short-lived tokens (≤15 min access) + refresh

**OAuth 2.0 + OIDC**
- Framework, not a token format — delegation of auth to an identity provider
- Tokens: access tokens (JWT or opaque), refresh tokens (long-lived), ID tokens (OIDC, always JWT for identity)
- **Best modern pattern**:
  - User → IdP (Okta, Auth0, AWS Cognito, Azure AD) → opaque access token to browser
  - Gateway/BFF introspects opaque token; mints short-lived internal JWT for microservices
  - Refresh tokens stored httpOnly Secure cookies; rotation on use
- **Grant types**: Authorization Code + PKCE for SPA/mobile; Client Credentials for service-to-service
- **Strengths**: standardized, ecosystem, delegation, SSO, MFA offloaded to IdP
- **Weaknesses**: complexity, correct implementation is subtle, many ways to misuse

**The modern hybrid (recommended)**
- **Edge**: opaque tokens (PASETO or opaque reference tokens) to browser — can be revoked instantly
- **Internal**: short-lived JWTs (≤5 min) between services — stateless, scales, revocation OK due to short lifetime
- **Refresh**: HttpOnly Secure, SameSite=Strict cookies; rotation on use; detect reuse
- **MFA**: on the IdP side; downstream services trust the IdP

**Pitfalls to avoid**
- Long-lived JWTs (days/weeks) without refresh — revocation nightmare
- Session cookies without `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite`
- JWT with weak HS256 shared secret
- Storing tokens in localStorage (XSS-exfiltratable)
- Rolling your own OAuth2 — use Spring Security OAuth2 / Keycloak / Auth0
- Missing audience / issuer claim checks
- Missing expiration / clock-skew handling

**When to pick what**
| Context | Best choice |
|---|---|
| Traditional server-rendered web app | Session + HttpOnly cookie |
| Microservices internal | Short-lived JWT |
| SPA + mobile + B2B | OAuth2 + OIDC via IdP |
| Regulated + SSO required | OIDC + enterprise IdP |
| Simple API key for ops | Long-lived opaque API key |

sections.title: Trade-offs, Anti-Patterns, and Sustainable Triage
sections.content:
**More scanners vs alert fatigue**
- 8 scanners with 2000 open findings = security theater; real bugs buried
- Curate rule sets; severity-based gating; triage discipline
- Fix false positives in rule config, not by ignoring findings
- Target: ≤ 50 open HIGH/CRITICAL findings at any time

**Shift-left vs shift-right**
- Shift-left: SAST/SCA in PR — cheapest fix, fastest feedback
- Shift-right: DAST/IAST/RASP/WAF — catches what left missed + runtime reality
- Do both; don't abandon one for the other

**Commercial vs open source**
- OSS: Semgrep, Trivy, Grype, OSV-Scanner, Checkov, ZAP, Gitleaks — excellent baseline
- Commercial: Snyk, CodeQL, Contrast — often better UX, integrations, reachability; check cost per dev
- Mix pragmatically; OSS first for baseline

**Precision vs recall**
- High recall (catches everything) = high FP rate = alert fatigue
- High precision (only real bugs) = misses some bugs
- Calibrate per tool; tune rules; measure FP rate and reduce over time

**Compliance vs real security**
- SOC 2 audit = process + evidence; doesn't mean secure
- Real security = culture, secure defaults, threat modeling, defense-in-depth
- Compliance as byproduct, not goal

**Centralized security team vs embedded**
- Centralized: consistent standards but bottleneck
- Embedded security champions in product teams: scale and velocity
- Both: central team sets standards, tooling, threat modeling; champions run day-to-day

**Session vs JWT dogma**
- "JWT is always stateless and scalable" — ignores revocation pain
- "Sessions don't scale" — Redis handles millions of sessions easily
- Pick based on actual requirements, not Twitter hot-takes

**Common anti-patterns**
1. **Scanner stacking without triage** — 8 tools, 2000 findings, nothing fixed
2. **Ignoring SCA** — dependency CVEs are the #1 real-world incident class
3. **JWT as god-token** (1-year lifetime, no refresh) — revocation impossible
4. **Storing tokens in localStorage** — XSS-exfiltratable
5. **SAST-only security** — misses OWASP Top 10 misconfigs
6. **DAST in CI on every PR** — too slow, blocks merges
7. **Rolling your own crypto / auth** — use Spring Security, OWASP ESAPI
8. **Suppressing findings without justification** — easier than fixing, bad culture
9. **Security team as gatekeeper** — embed champions, don't block
10. **Compliance-driven security** — checks boxes but misses threat modeling

**Senior engineer behaviors**
- **Threat model first** — what are we protecting, from whom, how?
- **Defense in depth** — multiple layers; one bypass doesn't pwn everything
- **Secure defaults** — input validation, parameterized queries, httponly cookies, TLS everywhere
- **SCA is table stakes** — dependency updates are the lowest-hanging fruit
- **Triage discipline** — target ≤ 50 open criticals; fix SLA defined
- **Security champions** in each product team; central team does tooling, threat modeling, IR
- **Tabletop exercises** — simulate leaked secret, account takeover, DDoS
- **Don't be the "department of no"** — offer secure paths, not just blocks

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Each scanner finds a different bug class** — none sufficient alone, more ≠ safer without triage
- **SAST**: source pattern analysis (Semgrep, CodeQL) — fast, noisy, PR-time
- **DAST**: running-app probing (ZAP, Burp) — slow, catches runtime issues
- **IAST**: runtime instrumentation (Contrast) — best accuracy, commercial, operational cost
- **SCA is the highest-ROI scanner** — dependency CVEs are #1 real-world incident class (Log4Shell, Spring4Shell)
- **Secrets scanning** (Gitleaks, TruffleHog) — pre-commit + CI + historical
- **Container scanning** (Trivy, Grype) at build; distroless + signing; rebuild weekly
- **IaC scanning** (Checkov, tfsec) catches open S3, permissive IAM at PR time
- **OWASP Top 10** = broad list; **ASVS** = tiered standard (target L2 for business, L3 for regulated)
- **SOC 2 / ISO 27001** audit process, not code; compliance ≠ real security
- **Session**: simplest, easy revoke, stateful; best for traditional web apps
- **JWT**: stateless scale, revocation hard; best short-lived internal microservice tokens
- **OAuth2 + OIDC**: delegation framework; opaque tokens at edge + internal JWTs is modern pattern
- **Anti-patterns**: scanner stacking without triage; long-lived JWTs; tokens in localStorage; ignoring SCA; compliance-driven security
- **Senior**: threat modeling, defense in depth, secure defaults, champions in product teams, secure-paved-path

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Each scanner finds a different bug class. None is sufficient alone. More tools without triage is security theater.

**Scanner map**
- SAST (Semgrep, SonarQube, CodeQL) — source pattern analysis — fast, PR-time, noisy
- SCA (Snyk, Dependabot, OSV-Scanner, Trivy) — dependency CVEs — highest ROI; real incidents are mostly dep CVEs
- DAST (ZAP, Burp) — runs against staging, catches runtime misconfigs SAST can't
- IAST (Contrast, Seeker) — runtime instrumentation, best accuracy, commercial
- Secrets scanning (Gitleaks, TruffleHog) — pre-commit + CI + historical
- Container scanning (Trivy, Grype) — OS + Java deps in images; run at build
- IaC scanning (Checkov, tfsec) — open S3, permissive IAM at PR time
- Runtime security (Falco, eBPF, RASP, WAF) — defense at runtime

**Practical pipeline for Java teams**
- PR CI: Semgrep + SCA + Secrets + IaC — must pass
- Weekly: CodeQL deep scan
- Nightly: SonarQube quality gates + ZAP against staging
- Build: container scan + Cosign signing + SBOM
- Runtime: Falco + Datadog ASM or Contrast
- Quarterly: human pentest on critical flows

**SAST specifics**
- Catches: SQL injection patterns, unsafe deserialization, crypto misuse, XSS sources/sinks
- Misses: logic flaws, misconfig, runtime state, deps
- Use PR-scoped, curated rule sets, severity gating
- Semgrep great FP rate and customizable; CodeQL deep

**DAST specifics**
- Runtime vulns: auth bypass, CSRF, session issues, cookie misconfigs, SSL
- Slow, needs staging, parameterized for logged-in flows, OpenAPI-aware
- Nightly not PR-time

**SCA — highest ROI**
- Log4Shell, Spring4Shell — real incidents are dep CVEs
- Reachability analysis cuts FPs 50–80%
- SBOM for supply-chain transparency
- Auto-merge low-risk patches with Renovate/Dependabot
- Block HIGH/CRITICAL without remediation plan

**Secrets**
- Pre-commit, CI, historical scan
- If leaked: rotate immediately, not suppress
- Preventive: Secrets Manager, Vault, no .env commits

**IaC**
- Checkov/tfsec on Terraform, CloudFormation, K8s YAML
- Catches 80% of misconfigs that cause breaches
- OPA/Gatekeeper enforces at runtime

**Frameworks (not scanners)**
- OWASP Top 10: broad list, minimum scanner coverage, training
- OWASP ASVS: tiered requirements — L1, L2, L3 — target L2 business, L3 regulated
- NIST 800-53: government contractors
- SOC 2 / ISO 27001: audit process, not code; compliance ≠ security
- CIS Benchmarks: hardening guides
- CWE/CVE: bug class taxonomy / specific vulns

**Session vs JWT vs OAuth2**

*Session (cookie + server store)*
- Simplest, easy to revoke, stateful
- Best traditional web apps

*JWT*
- Stateless scale, revocation pain, bloat
- Risks: alg:none, weak HS256, long lifetimes
- Best: short-lived (≤15 min) internal microservice tokens

*OAuth2 + OIDC*
- Framework for delegation; opaque tokens at edge, JWTs internal
- Auth Code + PKCE for SPA/mobile; Client Credentials for service-to-service
- Best for modern: delegate auth to IdP (Okta, Auth0, Cognito)

*Modern hybrid*
- Edge: opaque tokens (revocable)
- Internal: short-lived JWTs
- Refresh: HttpOnly Secure SameSite=Strict cookies, rotation on use
- MFA on IdP

**Pitfalls**
- Long-lived JWTs without refresh
- Cookies without HttpOnly/Secure/SameSite
- Tokens in localStorage (XSS exfil)
- Rolling own OAuth2
- Missing audience/issuer/expiration checks

**Trade-offs**
- More scanners vs alert fatigue — curate, triage, gate on severity
- Shift-left + shift-right — both; don't abandon one
- Commercial vs OSS — OSS baseline, commercial for UX/reachability
- Precision vs recall — tune rules, measure FP rate
- Compliance vs real security — compliance byproduct, not goal
- Centralized vs embedded — security champions in product teams
- Session vs JWT dogma — pick by actual requirements

**Anti-patterns**
- Scanner stacking without triage
- Ignoring SCA
- JWT god-token with year-long lifetime
- LocalStorage tokens
- SAST-only security
- DAST in every PR CI
- Rolling own crypto/auth
- Suppressing findings without justification
- Security team as gatekeeper
- Compliance-driven security

**Senior behaviors**
- Threat model first — what, from whom, how
- Defense in depth — multiple layers
- Secure defaults — validation, parameterized queries, HttpOnly cookies, TLS
- SCA as table stakes
- Triage discipline — ≤ 50 open criticals, fix SLA
- Security champions in product teams
- Tabletop exercises — leaked secret, account takeover, DDoS
- Offer secure paved paths, don't be department of no

**Bottom line**
- Pipeline: SAST + SCA + secrets + IaC in PR; DAST/IAST in staging; runtime security; human pentest
- SCA is the highest-ROI scanner
- ASVS is the real standard; OWASP Top 10 is the checklist
- Token format depends on context — edge opaque + internal short JWT is modern
- Security is culture + defaults + threat modeling, not stacking tools
